title: Educathons as participatory design sprints for responsible AI in teacher education
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly influences teaching and learning, yet design and adoption decisions often proceed with limited sustained input from educators and learners. This paper examines educathons as time-bounded interdisciplinary design sprints in teacher education. It reports a case study of a 3-day educathon held during the 2025 Summer School on Enhancing Education through Gamification and AI, where 50 prospective teachers worked in 10 mixed teams to prototype AI-enabled learning technology concepts. Using project appraisal, design artefacts, observation notes, survey responses and focus groups, this study reports descriptive and interpretive patterns related to prototype quality, interdisciplinary collaboration and ethical reasoning rather than causal learning effects. The findings indicate that teams produced pedagogically relevant prototypes, that interdisciplinary participation supported mutual learning and that ethical tensions related to fairness, explainability, automation bias and privacy shaped design trade-offs. title: Feedback, engagement, and integrative learning: a trace-based case study in a synchronous course
abstract: This case study examines how formative assessment performance, student engagement traces, and instructor feedback language co-vary with performance on a final integrative assessment. The study was conducted in a 12-week, second-year Framework for Higher Education Qualifications (FHEQ) Level 6) undergraduate course on empirical analysis and the scientific method (N = 49). We triangulate low-stakes assessments, platform-generated engagement indicators (talktime, hand raises, votes, reactions, and chat messages), and Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count 2022 (LIWC-22) features of instructor feedback. Psychological safety serves as a theoretical lens for interpreting students’ contributions, responses to feedback, and continued engagement after lower early formative scores; the empirical analysis rests entirely on observable assessment, participation, and feedback data. Classroom interaction data make some aspects of participation visible, but cannot, by themselves, reveal the learning conditions students experienced. title: Identifying the impact of active learning strategies on student satisfaction in physical and online environments
abstract: This study investigates the comparative efficacy of physical and online learning modalities in management education, focusing on student satisfaction and learning outcomes. It examines how improvements in Management Basics (MB), Management Organisation (MO), Management Techniques (MT), Problem-Based Learning (PBL), and Task-Based Learning (TBL) affect satisfaction across both environments. A quantitative research design involved 128 first-year management students in Taiwan across two semesters. Data from online and physical learning contexts were analysed using correlation and multiple regression to assess relationships between learning improvements and satisfaction. Regression analysis indicates that PBL exerts the strongest influence on satisfaction in both modalities, followed by TBL in physical learning. In online learning, MB and MO are key predictors, while MT and TBL show limited impact. The findings suggest that educators should prioritise PBL across both environments to enhance student satisfaction. title: Bridging technical and emotional skill gaps: AI-enhanced adaptive learning and emotional intelligence in project management education
Measuring what matters: a systematic review and VOSviewer-based bibliometric approach to digital literacy assessment instruments, competency dimensions and challenges in education
abstract: Digital literacy is a critical competency in education across all levels, from primary to higher education. It includes skills such as technical proficiency, information evaluation, online collaboration, creativity and ethical technology use. This study conducts a Systematic Literature Review (SLR), following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines, to examine types of instruments used to assess students’ digital literacy, the competencies targeted and the methodological challenges in their development. A total of 23 peer-reviewed articles published between 2014 and 2024 were selected from Scopus, PubMed, Crossref and ERIC. This review shows that assessment instruments include Likert scale-based questionnaires, framework-aligned tools (DigComp and DQ Framework) and digital performance-based methods. These instruments are applied across diverse educational settings: primary, secondary, tertiary and adult education with varying emphases based on age and learning context. title: A canonical correlation analysis of the influence of access to and use of ICT on secondary school students’ academic performance
abstract: This study was conducted to examine the influence of access to and use of information and communication technology (ICT) on academic achievement and motivation. Data were collected from 300 students (12- to 16-year-old; 160 boys) from Sanandaj, Iran. The ICT Familiarity Questionnaire was used to assess the level of students’ access to and use of ICT at school and outside of school. Students’ Grade Point Average was considered as an indicator of academic achievement and their scores of Academic Motivation Scale as a measure of academic motivation. The findings revealed that students had more access to and use of ICT at home than school. The majority of participants reported that they used digital devices for the first time when they were between 7 and 10 years old. The students spent more time using the Internet outside of school during weekdays. They used digital devices more frequently for general than academic activities. The canonical analysis indicated that ICT-related factors are significantly correlated with academic performance. title: The impact of online learning technology on self-regulation and student success
abstract: The research purpose is to analyse the self-regulation of students who use the massive open online course (MOOC) technology to learn the exact sciences. The sample included 252 students: females were 47%, and males were 53%. The average age of students was 20.08 ± 0.72. The students were divided into two groups: group 1 consisted of students who learnt the Digital singular (nano) optics course online using the MicrosoftTeams platform with teacher’s support; group 2 consisted of students who learnt the MOOC course individually. The relationships between self-regulation and academic success were also analysed. The research found that the overall level of self-regulation of students using MOOCs was 40% higher. title: Bridging the trust gap: a mixed-methods study of United Kingdom educators’ perceptions of generative artificial intelligence in higher education assessment
abstract: Situated against the backdrop of an evolving regulatory landscape, this study investigates the perceptions of United Kingdom university educators regarding the use of generative artificial intelligence in summative assessment. Through a mixed-methods survey of 330 academic staff, the research identifies a significant gap between high levels of digital literacy and low evaluative trust. While respondents report high familiarity with AI tools, confidence in the ability of artificial intelligence to provide fair or nuanced marks remains low. Qualitative analysis of open text questions reveals a nuance crisis, where educators perceive these systems as incapable of comprehending complex student submissions. The findings reveal significant gender disparities in technical proficiency, however, a consistent pattern of low evaluative trust persists across teaching experience levels, with no statistically significant differences detected based on professional seniority, suggesting a potential need to consider alternative pedagogical frameworks, such as performative and synchronous assessments, to safeguard academic integrity.
